The cithara is an instrument of the ancient Greek yoke-lute family and can be seen as the professional version of the lyre. It has a deep wooden soundbox, two flat or slightly arched soundboards joined by sides of even width; usually there are seven strings, fastened at one end to a crossbar or yoke and at the other through a flat bridge to the tailpiece. The player plucks the strings with a hard plectrum of dried hide and stops the strings that are not to sound with the left hand. It was played mainly by professionals to accompany dance, epic recitation, rhapsodies, hymns and lyric songs, and to play solo at banquets, receptions, state contests and competitions of skill.
演奏時，右手持乾燥皮革製成的硬撥，肘部伸展、手掌內彎，以撥弦發聲。左手伸直手指，: To play, hold a hard plectrum of dried hide in the right hand, elbow out and palm turned in, and pluck the strings. The left hand stretches out its fingers and presses the strings that are not to sound, to stop them. A beginner should concentrate on coordinating plucking and stopping so that all seven strings sound clearly.
